'''Michael Bruce Eisen''' (born April 13, 1967) is an American computational biologist and the former<ref>{{Cite news |last=Science News Staff |date=24 October 2023 |title=Prominent journal editor fired for endorsing satirical article about Israel-Hamas conflict |work=Science |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/prominent-journal-editor-fired-endorsing-satirical-article-israel-hamas |url-status=live |access-date=24 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231024021510/https://www.science.org/content/article/prominent-journal-editor-fired-endorsing-satirical-article-israel-hamas |archive-date=24 October 2023}}</ref> editor-in-chief of the journal [[eLife]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://elifesciences.org/inside-elife/7eb55710/elife-welcomes-michael-eisen-as-editor-in-chief|title=eLife welcomes Michael Eisen as Editor-in-Chief|date=2019-03-05|website=eLife|language=en|access-date=2019-03-05}}</ref> He is a professor of [[genetics]], [[genomics]] and [[Developmental biology|development]] at [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Michael B. ==Early life and education==

Born in Boston, Eisen and his brother [[Jonathan Eisen|Jonathan]] were raised in a family of scientists. Their grandfather was an [[X-ray crystallography|x-ray crystallographer]], their father, Howard Eisen a physician, and mother, Laura<ref name="Laura Eisen Washington Post">{{cite news|last1=Okie|first1=Susan|title=NIH SCIENTIST A SUICIDE AMID PROBE OF PAPER|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1987/02/14/nih-scientist-a-suicide-amid-probe-of-paper/e0cd2abe-4763-40f4-b839-8e86df4b2cbd/|newspaper=Washington Post|accessdate=7 February 2017}}</ref> a biochemist. They moved to [[Bethesda, Maryland]] when Eisen was four or five years old. The brothers spent summers in Long Island with their grandparents. Eisen states that he loved frogs and salamanders '"Even more than I have a frog fetish, I have a swamp fetish. I really like being in swamps."'  He was also very interested in math and was captain of the high school math team. Eisen graduated from [[Walt Whitman High School (Bethesda, Maryland)|Walt Whitman High School]] in 1985. Intending to major in mathematics at Harvard University, he realized that there [he may encounter] other more brilliant math students, it was a ''[[Good Will Hunting]]'' moment and he decided that he did not want to major in mathematics, '"You don't want to be Salieri to Mozart."' During his years at Harvard, Eisen worked on "unlocking the three-dimensional structures of proteins." He was shown a [[DNA microarray]] which taught him a '"new way of doing biology"'.<ref name="Mechanic Mother Jones">{{cite web|last1=Mechanic|first1=Michael|title=Steal This Research Paper! (You Already Paid for It.)|url=https://www.motherjones.com/media/2013/09/michael-eisen-plos-open-access-aaron-swartz|publisher=Mother Jones|accessdate=7 February 2017}}</ref>

Eisen completed his PhD at [[Harvard University]] in biophysics and a B.S. (also from Harvard) in Math.<ref name="Merc Krieger"/>  He was under the supervision of [[Don Craig Wiley]]<ref name="India Bio Science"/> while studying [[Influenza A virus]] Proteins.<ref name="eisenphd">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|first=Michael Bruce |last=Eisen|title=Structural Studies of Influenza A Virus Proteins|publisher=Harvard University |date=1996|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e2wAHwAACAAJ| authorlink=Michael Eisen|oclc=48938206}}</ref>

{{Cquote|There are things that are really really difficult, those are the kinds of problems you do want to work on. It's not that easy to tell the difference between impossible problems and a problem that is really really difficult. But learning to do so is critically important. - Things I learned from working with Pat Brown ([[Patrick O. Brown]]) - 2015<ref name="India Bio Science"/>
}}

After earning his doctorate, Eisen was a Postdoctoral Fellow at [[Stanford University]] in the lab of [[David Botstein]], where he most notably developed a method for interpreting gene expression data from microarrays. The seminal research publication that Eisen authored about this project has been cited over 16,000 times.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Eisen|first1=MB|last2=Spellman|first2=PT|last3=Brown|first3=PO|last4=Botstein|first4=D|title=Cluster analysis and display of genome-wide expression patterns|journal=Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A|date=8 December 1998|volume=95|issue=25|pages=14863–8|pmid=9843981|doi=10.1073/pnas.95.25.14863|pmc=24541|bibcode=1998PNAS...9514863E|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Baseball and biology ===

When Eisen lived in Tennessee he worked as a [[Sports commentator|play-by-play announcer]] for a minor league baseball team,<ref name="Merc Krieger"/> the [[Columbia Mules (Big South League)|Columbia Mules]]. He is <!-- 8===8 --> a self-proclaimed [[Red Sox]] fanatic.<ref name="Mechanic Mother Jones"/> He and computational biologist James Fraser recorded a video for iBiology about the role baseball statistics influenced their research. Their argument is that sequencing DNA is similar to scoring a baseball game, and that many computational biologists learned to think about science computations from an obsessive interest in baseball stats. The exercise of comparing a specific player's stats to a database of other similar players allows a baseball fan to predict future performance. This same system works with proteins and predicting functions. As tools are developed that break down and track all stats concerning baseball players, so will technology improve with genetics. With both baseball and genetics, tools are being developed that refine the models.<ref name="Fraser Eisen Baseball">{{cite web|title=James Fraser & Michael Eisen: Baseball Meets Biology|url=https://www.ibiology.org/ibiomagazine/issue-6/james-fraser-michael-eisen-baseball-meets-biology.html|website=Education|publisher=iBiology|accessdate=7 February 2017}}</ref>  In a lecture in 2015, Eisen stated that he received a computer from his grandfather for his twelfth birthday and spent the next five years teaching himself how to program so that he could keep track of baseball stats.<ref name="India Bio Science">{{cite web|title=Michael Eisen: Baseball, mathematics and biology| date=31 August 2015 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BACy6Lsi6-U |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/BACy6Lsi6-U |archive-date=2021-12-21 |url-status=live|publisher=India Bio Science|accessdate=7 February 2017}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

==2018 U.S. Senate race==
{{main|2018 United States Senate election in California}}
Eisen announced through Twitter on January 25 his intent to run for U.S. Senate from California in 2018 for Democratic Senator [[Dianne Feinstein]]'s seat, registering the Twitter handle ''SenatorPhD''.<ref name="Reardon Nature">{{cite journal|url=http://www.nature.com/news/geneticist-launches-bid-for-us-senate-1.21381|title=Geneticist launches bid for US Senate|last1=Reardon|first1=Sara|journal=Nature|accessdate=7 February 2017|doi=10.1038/nature.2017.21381|year=2017|s2cid=78431422|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> His campaign slogan was "Liberty, Equality, Reality". Eisen's reasons for running for Congress included his perception that the [[Donald Trump|Trump administration]] was unresponsive to [[climate change]] and other science-related issues. Another reason Eisen decided to run was his experience watching Cabinet appointees being interviewed by the Senate about climate change. He thought '“It would be really nice to have scientists ask the questions of the Cabinet appointees, because the senators don’t seem to understand the issue and aren’t asking the right questions.”'<ref name="Merc Krieger" /> He feels that if science is to be on the forefront of policy making, '"scientists need to run for office."' He felt that 2018's California [[jungle primaries]] afforded him a better chance at making the final two for the general election, but he did not make the final two (which were Dianne Feinstein and [[Kevin de León]]).<ref name="Merc Krieger">{{cite web|last1=Krieger|first1=Lisa|title=Bay Area molecular biologist Michael Eisen announces bid for U.S. Senate|url=http://www.mercurynews.com/2017/02/03/bay-area-molecular-biologist-michael-eisen-announces-bid-for-u-s-senate/|website=San Jose Mercury News|accessdate=7 February 2017|date=2017-02-04}}</ref>

{{Cquote|For a really long time, scientists have watched political processes erode — and have watched politicians openly deride science, dismissing the role that science plays in our everyday life. Scientists have been sitting here hoping that someone would come along and defend those principals. Politics, in my mind, should function similar to science. We should try to figure out what’s going on in the world and then debate the best way to do it, to make the world better. The best tools we have to characterize reality are the observational tools that science uses all the time. Too much of politics has rejected that basic principle that scientists live and breathe all the time.<ref name="Merc Krieger"/>}}
Eisen dropped out of the race when he failed to qualify for the June 2018 primary ballot.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Michael_Eisen|title=Michael Eisen|website=Ballotpedia|language=en|access-date=2020-04-13}}</ref>

== ''eLife'' editorship and firing ==
In 2019, Eisen was named the second editor-in-chief of the open-access scientific journal ''eLife''.

In 2020, in response to a [[Twitter]] question, Eisen joked that the roundworm ''[[C. elegans]]'' was the most over-hyped animal because "they wiggle forward. They wiggle backwards. And occasionally they fuck themselves. That’s it". Some researchers were not amused by the joke, and the ''eLife'' board asked Eisen to watch his language on Twitter.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jones |first1=Asher |last2=Elbein |first2=Tyler O. |date=2 August 2020 |title=Worm Joke Causes Science Twitter Flame War Over Accusations of Sexism and Racism |url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/worm-joke-causes-science-twitter-flame-war-over-accusations-of-sexism-and-racism |access-date=22 August 2024 |website=The Daily Beast |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Mechanic |first=Michael |date=November 17, 2023 |title=A Top Science Journal Fired Its Editor Over a Pro-Palestinian Tweet. He Has No Regrets. |url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2023/11/michael-eisen-tweet-elife-firing-science-editor-palestinians-israel-gaza/ |access-date=August 31, 2024 |website=Mother Jones}}</ref> Also in 2020, Eisen was involved in the story surrounding the death from SARS-CoV-2 of an anonymous queer Hopi female professor with whom he had interacted on Twitter. The account turned out to be a hoax created and run by neuroscientist [[BethAnn McLaughlin]], who founded MeTooSTEM. Eisen was one of three people to attend a [[Zoom (software)|Zoom]] memorial for the fictional individual.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bromwich |first1=Jonah E. |last2=Marcus |first2=Ezra |date=4 August 2020 |title=The Anonymous Professor Who Wasn't |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/08/04/style/college-coronavirus-hoax.html |access-date=22 August 2024 |website=The New York Times}}</ref>

In 2023, under his leadership, the journal moved away from the traditional "[[Academic publishing|review, then publish]]" model, instead requiring authors to submit [[preprint]]s and then publishing journal editors' [[Peer review|reviews]] alongside manuscripts, meaning that the journal neither accepted nor rejected submissions.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Brainard |first=Jeffrey |date=20 October 2022 |title=Journal seeks to upend scientific publishing by only reviewing—not accepting—manuscripts |work=Science News |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/journal-seeks-upend-scientific-publishing-only-reviewing-not-accepting-manuscripts |access-date=24 October 2023}}</ref> Eisen said that the move was intended to reduce the prominence of the publisher, and instead focus attention on authors and their work. This move provoked both enthusiastic praise from some, including some ''eLife'' editors, and a strong backlash from others inside the organization, including some senior editors and editors. A news article in the journal Nature described the “Strife at eLife”. At least one of five deputy editors resigned. In a private letter to Eisen in January 2023, 30 editors threatened to resign once the changes were fully implemented. In March 2023, 29 ''eLife'' editors, including founding editor-in-chief and Nobel Prize winner [[Randy Schekman]], urged that Eisen should be replaced immediately in a letter to the executive editor of the journal’s publisher. Eisen dismissed this in an interview as “powerful scientists not wanting to change a system that has benefited them”. Eisen tweeted on March 12, 2023, that academics were "lobbying hard to get me fired", a post that was subsequently deleted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Abbott |first=Alison |date=17 March 2023 |title=Strife at eLife: inside a journal's quest to upend science publishing |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-00831-6 |access-date=27 August 2024 |journal=Nature |volume=615 |issue=7954 |pages=780–781 |doi=10.1038/d41586-023-00831-6 |pmid=36932204 |bibcode=2023Natur.615..780A |url-access=subscription }}</ref> He later described his relationship with the board as “somewhat testy” and that some “had it in for me”.<ref name=":3" />

On October 13, 2023, soon after [[Hamas]] attacked Israel, Eisen tweeted a story from by the [[Satire|satirical]] website ''[[The Onion]]'' with the headline: "Dying Gazans Criticized For Not Using Last Words To Condemn Hamas." Eisen said "The Onion speaks with more courage, insight and moral clarity than the leaders of every academic institution put together. I wish there were a @TheOnion university".<ref name="science241023">{{cite web |title=Prominent journal editor fired for endorsing satirical article about Israel-Hamas conflict |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/prominent-journal-editor-fired-endorsing-satirical-article-israel-hamas |website=Science |access-date=22 August 2024 |date=23 October 2023}}</ref> The post prompted some criticism, including from Israeli researchers who asked colleagues to avoid publishing in ''eLife'' as long as he was editor. The chair of ''eLife''’s board asked Eisen to delete his Twitter post, but he refused to do so "because that would be capitulating to what I thought was a really misdirected effort to silence any expression of support of Palestinians". On October 23, 2023, Eisen was fired by ''eLife''. In response to the firing, at least five of ''eLife''<nowiki/>'s editors resigned and other scientists said they would stop participating in ''eLife'' events in solidarity with Eisen. A petition letter was organised to protest against Eisen’s firing. The petition, which was signed by over 2,000 scientists, academics and researchers, said ''eLife''<nowiki/>'s action is having a "chilling effect" on freedom of expression in academia.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-26 |title=Firing of science journal editor after Gaza post sparks free speech rift |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/science/science-news/firing-science-journal-editor-gaza-post-sparks-free-speech-rift-rcna122128 |access-date=2023-11-01 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref>

''eLife'' released a statement saying "Mike has been given clear feedback from the board that his approach to leadership, communication and social media has at key times been detrimental to the cohesion of the community we are trying to build and hence to ''eLife''’s mission. It is against this background that a further incidence of this behaviour has contributed to the board’s decision".<ref name="science241023" /> Eisen's response was "They were referring to that fucking worm thing. I’m not even kidding!".<ref name=":3" /> An ''eLife'' spokesperson clarified in an email to ''The Hindu'', saying “We value and respect everyone’s right to freedom of speech including political expression and the legal right to protest. Particularly for those in leadership positions, exercising that right comes with responsibilities: an expectation to show good judgement and a duty of care to the communities they serve. We don’t believe those qualities have been demonstrated.”<ref>{{Cite web |last=Prasad |first=R |date=October 28, 2023 |title='eLife grieves the tragic losses of civilian lives, both Israeli and Palestinian' |url=https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/elife-grieves-the-tragic-losses-of-civilian-lives-both-israeli-and-palestinian/article67466064.ece |access-date=September 18, 2024 |website=The Hindu}}</ref>

In ''eLife’s'' 2023 annual report, the Chair of the Board of Directors said: “In October, we parted ways with our Editor-in-Chief, Michael Eisen, and want to acknowledge the extraordinary vision and leadership he provided to eLife, which is allowing us to build on his legacy as we grow our publishing model.”<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hackett |first=Joanne |date=September 5, 2024 |title=Annual Report: 2023 in review |url=https://elifesciences.org/inside-elife/e3e8def1/annual-report-2023-in-review |access-date=September 18, 2024 |website=eLife}}</ref>

On November 10, 2023, in response to a tweet saying “How to make faculty meeting more exciting? Wrong answers only.”, Eisen tweeted “Sit me next to Randy Schekman.”, indicating an ongoing personal conflict with the preceding [[Randy Schekman|editor-in-chief]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Eisen |first=Michael |date=November 10, 2023 |title=Twitter |url=https://x.com/mbeisen/status/1723048624622322155 |access-date=October 24, 2024 |website=Twitter}}</ref>

==Open access advocacy==
Throughout his career he has been an advocate for "[[open science]]", which is the free release of the material and intellectual product of scientific research. He is a leading advocate of [[Open access (publishing)|open access scientific publishing]]<ref>{{cite news|last=Eisen|first=Michael|title=Publish and be praised|url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2003/oct/09/research.highereducation|accessdate=23 September 2013|newspaper=Guardian|date=8 October 2003}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Brown | first1 = P. O. | authorlink1 = Patrick O. Brown| last2 = Eisen | first2 = M. B. | authorlink2 = Michael Eisen| last3 = Varmus | first3 = H. E. | authorlink3 = Harold E. Varmus| title = Why PLoS Became a Publisher | doi = 10.1371/journal.pbio.0000036 | journal = PLOS Biology | volume =  1| issue = 1 | pages =  E36| year = 2003 | pmid =  14551926| pmc = 212706 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |author=WIRED Staff |title=The 2004 Wired Rave Awards |language=en-US |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/2004/04/rave/ |access-date=2023-08-11 |issn=1059-1028}}</ref> and is co-founder of [[PLOS|Public Library of Science (PLOS)]] and serves on the PLOS board, the Academic Steering & Advocacy Committee of [[Open Library of Humanities]],<ref>{{cite journal|last=Howard|first=Jennifer|title=Project Aims to Bring PLoS-Style Openness to the Humanities|url=http://chronicle.com/article/Project-Aims-to-Bring/136889/|journal=The Chronicle of Higher Education|accessdate=19 November 2013|date=29 January 2013}}</ref> and is an adviser to [[Science Commons]].

In 2012 Eisen began protesting against the [[Research Works Act]] as part of his appeal to promote open access to information.<ref>{{cite magazine |url= https://www.wired.com/2012/01/congress-considers-paywalling-science-you-already-paid-for/ |title=Congress Considers Paywalling Science You Already Paid For |first=David |last=Dobbs |magazine=wired.com |date=6 January 2012 |access-date=12 February 2012}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
In 2002, Eisen was awarded the inaugural [[Benjamin Franklin Award (Bioinformatics)|Benjamin Franklin Award]] in bioinformatics, for his work on [[PLOS]] and the open-access availability of his microarray cluster analysis software.<ref name="franklin-award">{{cite web|title=Benjamin Franklin Award - Bioinformatics.org|url=http://www.bioinformatics.org/franklin/|website=www.bioinformatics.org|accessdate=7 February 2017|language=en}}</ref>
